sub_themes.sub_theme: Membrane protein trafficking in patient fibroblasts

insights.claim: Perinuclear accumulation of a membrane protein in patient fibroblasts may reflect altered trafficking, but alternatives remain untested.
Imaging-based mislocalization rates show where a protein sits, not whether its trafficking function is impaired.
Testing a trafficking defect needs a functional assay, with controls separating real effects from assay artifacts; design expertise is required.
Repeated LLM extraction of variant-phenotype mentions from one paper yields differing lists, with recall the unstable component.
Cross-run agreement can triage LLM extractions: consistent items accepted, inconsistent ones sent to logged human review.

adjacent_ideas.claim: An agreement-scored LLM extraction pipeline could compile reported localization and trafficking phenotypes for the protein across related diseases.
The same agreement-and-review logic could quantify reliability of mislocalization calls across repeated or independent image scoring.
Systematically extracting published trafficking assay designs could shortlist feasible readouts and controls for patient fibroblasts.

insights.claim: Mislocalized transporter signal by imaging does not by itself establish that transport function has changed.
Substrate uptake, surface labelling and pulse-chase should be compared with localization in the same cells rather than imaging alone.
Holding a transporter in the ER then releasing it synchronously can time delivery to the plasma membrane in disease versus control cells.
Apparently slower surface arrival stays preliminary until it reproduces across cell lines and conditions.
A reporter tag may itself slow transport, so a second independent tag or untagged construct is needed.
Arrival-rate comparisons require matched expression between disease and control cells, via sorting or inducible promoters.
A pathway-blocking condition plus an unaffected control cargo distinguishes a real trafficking defect from assay artifact.

adjacent_ideas.claim: Whether measured surface-arrival delays predict quantitative loss of substrate uptake, or are compensated by residual steady-state surface pool.
Surface biotinylation or antibody-accessibility time courses could time delivery without relying on a potentially rate-altering fluorescent tag.
Slower arrival could reflect ER retention and turnover rather than slowed transit, separable by blocking degradation pathways.
